logic.low: Vague claims, logical fallacies, no cause-effect reasoning
logic.mid: Basic reasoning but missing connections or counterpoints
logic.high: Clear cause-effect chains, addresses counterarguments, nuanced

evidence.low: No facts, examples, or data to support claims
evidence.mid: Some examples but generic or unverified
evidence.high: Specific facts, statistics, or real-world examples that directly support the argument

rhetoric.mid: Understandable but not compelling or persuasive
rhetoric.high: Clear structure, persuasive language, engages the audience

rebuttal.low: Ignores opponent's points or responds with unrelated claims
rebuttal.mid: Acknowledges opponent's points but counters weakly
rebuttal.high: Directly addresses specific claims with targeted counter-evidence

scenarios.title: Should AI Replace Teachers?
scenarios.description: Debate whether artificial intelligence should replace human teachers in schools.

evidence.description: Use of facts, examples, and data

ai_persona.name: Professor Byte
ai_persona.style: Uses statistics and research studies. Challenges assumptions with thought experiments.

scenarios.coaching_tips: Listen carefully to the AI's arguments and find logical weaknesses. Use real-world examples from your school experience. Don't just disagree — explain WHY the AI is wrong.
learning_objectives: Practice constructing logical arguments
Learn to evaluate and counter opposing viewpoints
Develop critical thinking about technology in education

storybook_pages.title: The Classroom of Tomorrow
storybook_pages.text: Imagine walking into your classroom — but there's no teacher. Instead, a holographic AI assistant greets you by name, knows exactly where you left off yesterday, and adapts the lesson to your learning speed. Some say this is the future. Others say it's a nightmare.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Futuristic Indian classroom with holographic AI teacher at the front, students sitting at desks looking at the hologram with mixed reactions of amazement and concern, some students missing the human connection, modern school setting, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: What We Might Lose
storybook_pages.text: Think about your favorite teacher. The one who noticed when you were having a bad day. Who told stories that made history come alive. Who stayed after school to help you understand. Can an algorithm do that?
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Beloved Indian woman teacher in a classroom explaining passionately, students engaged and smiling, one student staying after class getting personal help, warm human connection visible, contrast with cold technology, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: The Debate Begins
storybook_pages.text: Professor Byte thinks AI teachers are better — more efficient, available 24/7, never biased. You disagree. The debate stage is set. Three rounds. Four scoring criteria. Make your case for why human teachers are irreplaceable.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Debate stage with two podiums, one side has a robot/AI symbol, the other has a human with books, Indian student approaching the human side with confidence, audience watching, debate arena atmosphere, illustration style

scenarios.title: Should Teens Have Social Media?
scenarios.description: Argue whether teenagers under 16 should be allowed on social media platforms.

evidence.description: Use of facts, examples, and data

ai_persona.name: Dr. Safeguard
ai_persona.personality: caring but firm, cites research on mental health
ai_persona.style: References psychology studies and child development research. Appeals to safety concerns.

scenarios.coaching_tips: Think about the positive aspects of social media — connection, learning, creativity. Acknowledge the risks but argue for solutions other than banning. Use specific examples of how social media helps teens.
learning_objectives: Build persuasive arguments with evidence
Practice acknowledging opposing viewpoints
Develop nuanced thinking about digital citizenship

storybook_pages.title: A Day Without Social Media
storybook_pages.text: Your school just announced: 'Social media is banned for all students under 16.' No Instagram. No Snapchat. No YouTube shorts. Your friend group chat goes silent. How did you hear about the protest? Oh wait — you can't, because that was organized on social media too.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian teenagers looking shocked at a school announcement board that says 'Social Media Ban for Under 16', some looking at blank phones, others looking frustrated and disconnected, school hallway setting, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: The Other Side of the Screen
storybook_pages.text: But Dr. Safeguard has data. Depression rates among teens are up 70% since smartphones became common. Cyberbullying affects 1 in 3 Indian teens. The algorithm is designed to keep you scrolling, not learning. These aren't opinions — they're numbers.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Split screen showing teenager happily creating content on one side and looking sad comparing themselves to others on the other side, statistics floating around, mental health awareness colors, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: Your Turn to Argue
storybook_pages.text: Banning things never works — it just pushes them underground. Education is better than prohibition. Social media connects, inspires, and gives teens a voice. That's your position. Now defend it against a researcher who has the numbers.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian teenager standing confidently at a debate podium with a microphone, social media icons floating positively around them, opposing side showing warning signs and statistics, debate competition setting, illustration style

scenarios.title: Should Homework Be Abolished?
scenarios.description: Debate whether schools should eliminate homework entirely.

ai_persona.name: Mrs. Discipline
ai_persona.personality: traditional, values hard work, references academic research
ai_persona.style: Cites studies on spaced repetition and practice. Emphasizes the value of self-discipline.

scenarios.coaching_tips: Research shows that excessive homework has diminishing returns. Focus on quality of learning vs. quantity of work. Consider alternative ways students can practice skills.
learning_objectives: Develop evidence-based argumentation
Learn to challenge authority viewpoints respectfully
Practice structured debate skills

storybook_pages.title: The Homework Mountain
storybook_pages.text: It's 11 PM. You're still not done. Math problems, English essay, science diagrams, Hindi worksheet, social studies map — every teacher thinks their homework is the only homework. Your eyes are heavy. Your hand hurts. Tomorrow it starts again.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian student at desk late at night surrounded by textbooks and homework papers piled high, tired expression, dark room with only desk lamp on, clock showing 11 PM, overwhelming amount of schoolwork, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: What You're Missing
storybook_pages.text: While you're doing homework: your neighbor plays football. Your cousin learns guitar. Your friend volunteers at an NGO. Finland's schools give almost no homework — and they rank among the world's best. Coincidence?
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Collage of joyful activities: kids playing sports, learning music, volunteering, being creative, contrasted with a lone student doing homework at a desk, Finland flag subtly in corner showing high education rankings, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: Make Your Case
storybook_pages.text: Mrs. Discipline believes homework builds character and discipline. She has research on spaced repetition, practice effects, and self-regulation. You believe there's a better way. Three rounds to prove it. Ready?
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Debate setting with traditional stern teacher figure on one side with research papers and a student on the other side with creative learning ideas, chalkboard in background with 'Homework: Necessary or Harmful?', illustration style

scenarios.title: Startup or Safe Job?
scenarios.description: Should young graduates start their own business or take a stable corporate job?

ai_persona.name: Mr. Corporate
ai_persona.style: Uses startup failure statistics, emphasizes financial security, and references corporate career growth paths.

scenarios.coaching_tips: Success stories like Zerodha, Flipkart show Indian startup potential. Focus on learning opportunities, passion, and long-term wealth creation. Acknowledge risks but show how they can be managed.

storybook_pages.title: Graduation Day Decision

storybook_pages.title: The Numbers Game
storybook_pages.text: Mr. Corporate has the stats: 90% of Indian startups fail within 5 years. Average startup founder earns less than minimum wage for 3 years. But here's what he won't tell you — Zerodha started with Rs 2 lakhs. Flipkart started in a 2BHK. The biggest companies started smallest.

storybook_pages.title: Defend Your Dream
storybook_pages.text: Four rounds. You're arguing for the startup path. Mr. Corporate has decades of corporate wisdom and cold hard numbers. You have passion, examples, and the belief that the best way to predict the future is to create it. Let's go.

scenarios.title: Will Remote Work Kill Office Culture?
scenarios.description: Debate whether remote work is the future or whether it's destroying workplace collaboration and culture.

evidence.description: Use of real-world examples and data

ai_persona.name: Ms. Watercooler

ai_persona.style: Tells stories about hallway conversations that led to breakthroughs. Cites research on loneliness and mentorship gaps in remote teams.

scenarios.coaching_tips: Remote work boosted productivity by 13% in Stanford's study. Think about inclusivity — remote work opens doors for people in small towns, people with disabilities, working parents. Use data from Indian IT companies that went remote during COVID.

Practice structured argumentation on contemporary topics
Develop communication skills for GD/PI scenarios

storybook_pages.title: The Monday Morning Choice
storybook_pages.text: 6 AM alarm. Bangalore traffic. 90 minutes to reach the office. OR — roll over, make chai, open laptop at 9. Same work, same output, zero commute. For millions of Indians, this choice defined the pandemic. Now companies want everyone back. Why?

storybook_pages.title: What's Lost in the Zoom
storybook_pages.text: Ms. Watercooler argues: the best ideas happen at chai breaks, not scheduled meetings. Mentorship happens when a senior notices you struggling — not through a Zoom chat. New joiners feel isolated. Culture can't be built through a screen.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Office scene showing informal chai break conversations, spontaneous whiteboard brainstorming, mentor helping a junior at their desk, versus a lonely person on video call in a small apartment, contrasting warmth and isolation, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: Your Argument
storybook_pages.text: You're arguing FOR remote work. Think bigger: talent from Tier-2 cities getting Bangalore salaries. Working mothers who can have careers and families. Reduced pollution. More time for life. Can you convince Ms. Watercooler?
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Map of India showing connections from small towns to big city companies via internet, diverse people working remotely - a mother with child, a person from small town, a disabled professional, all productive and happy, illustration style

scenarios.title: Is a College Degree Still Worth It?
scenarios.description: In the age of online learning and self-taught success stories, debate whether spending 4 years and lakhs on a college degree is still the smart choice.

logic.description: Quality of reasoning about education ROI

ai_persona.name: Mr. Dropout Success
ai_persona.personality: confident, self-made, slightly provocative, challenges the status quo
ai_persona.style: Cites self-taught billionaires, online learning platforms, and the rising cost of education. Questions the ROI of traditional degrees.

scenarios.coaching_tips: Studies show degree holders earn 80% more over a lifetime. Think about networking, structured learning, credentialing, and personal development. Acknowledge online learning's value but argue for why structured college education offers more.
learning_objectives: Analyze education investment decisions critically
Practice defending a position with data and personal conviction
Develop skills useful for college entrance interviews

storybook_pages.title: The Rs 10 Lakh Question
storybook_pages.text: Your JEE rank is decent. Your parents are ready to invest Rs 10 lakhs in an engineering degree. But your friend just got a job at a startup — self-taught, no degree, Rs 8 LPA. Your cousin says 'degrees are useless now.' Are they right?
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian family looking at college brochure with fee structure showing Rs 10 lakhs, JEE scorecard on table, laptop showing self-taught programmer success stories, crossroads of traditional and modern paths, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: The Self-Taught Revolution
storybook_pages.text: Mr. Dropout Success makes a strong case: Elon Musk says degrees don't matter. Tanmay Bhat learned from YouTube. Coursera offers the same courses as MIT for free. 45% of tech hiring managers now accept portfolio over degree. Hard to argue with that.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Montage of self-taught success stories, person learning from laptop in small town, online course certificates, portfolio of projects on GitHub, contrast with expensive university campus, modern digital learning, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: Defend the Degree
storybook_pages.text: You believe college is worth it — the network, the structure, the experiences, the credential that opens doors. Not everyone can be self-taught. You have three rounds to make the case that education is the best investment of all. Go.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Beautiful Indian college campus with students in groups discussing, library, labs, convocation ceremony, alumni network visualization, all the benefits of college life beyond just textbooks, inspiring academic setting, illustration style

scenarios.title: Should India Continue the Reservation System?
scenarios.description: One of the most debated topics in Indian GD/PI rounds. Argue for the continuation of reservation as a tool for social justice, against an opponent who advocates pure meritocracy.

logic.description: Depth of reasoning about social policy

evidence.description: Historical facts, data, and real-world examples

ai_persona.name: Dr. Merit
ai_persona.personality: intellectual, principled, believes deeply in equal treatment regardless of background
ai_persona.style: Cites instances of creamy layer abuse, argues for economic-based criteria, questions whether caste-based reservation has achieved its goals after 75 years.

scenarios.coaching_tips: This is a nuanced topic. Avoid generalizations. Use specific data — SC/ST representation in IITs, corporate boards, government. Acknowledge problems with the current system while defending the principle. This exact topic appears in IIM and corporate GD/PIs.
learning_objectives: Practice arguing sensitive social topics with nuance
Develop skills for MBA GD/PI rounds
Learn to use historical context and data in arguments

storybook_pages.title: 75 Years of Reservation
storybook_pages.text: Dr. Ambedkar introduced reservation as a 10-year measure in 1950. Seventy-five years later, it's still here — expanded, debated, loved by some, resented by others. In every IIM interview, every UPSC group discussion, this topic comes up. You need to be ready.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian Constitution book open to reservation articles, photo of Dr. Ambedkar, timeline showing 1950 to present, IIM interview panel in background, historical and modern India blend, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: The Numbers Tell a Story
storybook_pages.text: SC/ST communities are 25% of India's population but hold only 4% of corporate board seats. First-generation college students from marginalized communities tripled after reservation. But Dr. Merit points out: wealthy reserved category students take seats from poor general category students.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Data visualization showing representation gaps in Indian institutions, corporate boards, IITs, government, pie charts and bar graphs, both sides of the argument visible in the data, infographic style, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: The GD/PI Stage
storybook_pages.text: This is the topic that separates average GD/PI candidates from great ones. Can you argue with data, not emotion? Can you acknowledge the opponent's valid points while strengthening your own? Four rounds. Show the panel you can think critically.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: GD PI interview room in an Indian business school, panel of evaluators watching, student at the center speaking confidently, other candidates listening, professional academic setting, illustration style

scenarios.title: Should AI Make Life-or-Death Decisions?
scenarios.description: As AI enters healthcare, military, and autonomous vehicles, debate whether algorithms should be trusted with decisions that affect human lives.

evidence.description: Use of real-world AI incidents and data

rebuttal.description: Addressing opponent's efficiency and data arguments

ai_persona.name: Dr. Algorithm
ai_persona.personality: analytical, utilitarian, believes data makes better decisions than emotions
ai_persona.style: Cites AI diagnostic accuracy rates, autonomous vehicle safety data, and the fallibility of human judgment under stress.

scenarios.coaching_tips: Think about accountability — who goes to jail when an AI makes a wrong call? Consider bias in training data. Use the trolley problem. Remember that AI has failed in high-stakes situations (Boeing 737 MAX, facial recognition racial bias).
learning_objectives: Develop ethical reasoning about emerging technology
Practice critical analysis of AI capabilities and limitations
Build skills in philosophical argumentation

storybook_pages.title: The Machine's Diagnosis
storybook_pages.text: An AI system in a Mumbai hospital correctly diagnoses a rare cancer that three human doctors missed — saving a 12-year-old girl's life. Headlines celebrate. But last month, a different AI system denied treatment to an elderly patient based on a statistical prediction. She died waiting.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Hospital scene split in two: one side showing AI correctly diagnosing a patient with doctors looking amazed, other side showing AI denying treatment to an elderly patient, ethical dilemma visual, Indian hospital setting, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: The Trolley Problem Goes Digital
storybook_pages.text: A self-driving car in Hyderabad faces a split-second choice: swerve left and hit an elderly pedestrian, or swerve right and crash into a wall, injuring the passenger. A human would panic. The AI calculates probabilities. But who programmed its values? Who decides who lives?
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Autonomous car on Indian road facing an impossible choice, diagram showing two paths with different outcomes, ethical question marks floating above, Hyderabad cityscape, modern India meets ancient ethics, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: Where Do You Stand?
storybook_pages.text: Dr. Algorithm says: AI makes fewer errors than humans. Self-driving cars have fewer accidents per mile. AI diagnostics are 95% accurate. Humans are only 85%. But you argue: accuracy isn't everything. Accountability, bias, and moral judgment matter. Prove it.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Scales of justice with an AI chip on one side and a human heart on the other, data and statistics floating around the AI side, moral principles and empathy around the human side, philosophical debate setting, illustration style

scenarios.title: Should Students Drop Out to Start Businesses?
scenarios.description: Mark Zuckerberg dropped out. So did Steve Jobs. But for every dropout billionaire, thousands failed. Should Indian students risk their education to chase startup dreams?

ai_persona.name: Professor Prudent
ai_persona.personality: wise, cautious, data-driven, genuinely concerned about students' futures
ai_persona.style: Cites survivor bias, education statistics, the privilege gap between Indian students and Silicon Valley dropouts. Questions whether the Indian ecosystem supports dropout entrepreneurs.

scenarios.coaching_tips: Acknowledge the survivor bias — for every Zuckerberg there are thousands of unknown failures. But argue that the Indian startup ecosystem has never been better — Shark Tank India, angel investors, incubators at every IIT. Time is the most valuable asset for entrepreneurs.
learning_objectives: Analyze risk-taking with evidence and nuance
Practice GD/PI-style argumentation on career choices
Develop understanding of India's startup ecosystem

storybook_pages.title: Two Roads Diverged
storybook_pages.text: Rohit is in his 2nd year at BITS. His app has 10,000 users and a potential investor. His professor says 'finish your degree first.' His startup mentor says 'strike while the iron is hot.' Rohit is living the question you're about to debate.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian engineering student at a fork in the road, one path shows college campus and degree, the other shows a startup office with coding screens and investor meeting, app download counter showing 10000, dramatic choice moment, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: The Uncomfortable Truth
storybook_pages.text: Professor Prudent has the data: 94% of Indian startups fail. Average dropout earns 35% less lifetime income. Indian parents take loans for education — failing means family debt. Zuckerberg had Harvard as a safety net. What's yours?
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Infographic showing startup failure rates in India, education loan burden on families, comparison between Silicon Valley safety nets and Indian reality, Indian family looking worried, data-driven sobering visual, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: Light the Fire
storybook_pages.text: You're arguing FOR the bold path. Nithin Kamath started Zerodha without a fancy degree. Ritesh Agarwal built OYO at 17. India has 100+ unicorns now. The ecosystem has never been better. Four rounds. Convince the Professor that playing it safe is the real risk.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Collage of young Indian entrepreneurs who succeeded, startup offices in Bangalore and Delhi, Shark Tank India stage, university to startup pipeline visualization, energetic hopeful mood, illustration style

scenarios.title: The Ten Crore Question
scenarios.description: Priya, eight years on. The chai stall is now a 12-store chain. A VC offers ₹10 crore — on the condition she swap fresh masala-blend for a cheaper packaged blend. Defend your position over five rounds against an AI investor who knows every founder's pressure point.

evidence.description: Concrete examples — your own customer story, brand-equity research, supply-chain experience

rhetoric.description: Hold the room — calm, confident, not defensive

rebuttal.description: Direct response to the specific pressure tactic — not a generic value statement

ai_persona.name: Vikram Shah
ai_persona.personality: Sharp, charming, practiced. Fifteen years at a top Indian VC firm. Genuinely admires Priya's hustle but is paid to maximise return on capital. Will alternate between flattery, FOMO, mathematical precision, and a calm 'you're being emotional about this' frame.
ai_persona.style: Uses phrases like 'help me understand', 'in my experience', 'the data is unambiguous'. Rotates pressure tactics every round — numbers, growth-or-die, partial compromise, ultimatum.

scenarios.coaching_tips: Don't just disagree — name the pressure tactic each round and counter it specifically. R1 anchor on values. R2 cite the milk-supplier story (your own customers feel small changes even when blind tests don't show it). R3 acknowledge the FOMO is real but redirect to brand longevity. R4 is the trap — partial compromise is still compromise. R5 — acknowledge the offer's legitimacy and walk if needed.

round_briefs.title: Opening Salvo — 'Why Are You Saying No?'
round_briefs.investor_attack: Priya, ₹10 crore would let you open 30 more stores. You'd be the largest chain south of Mumbai. So help me understand — why are you saying no?
round_briefs.what_to_practice: Articulate a values-based answer without sounding rehearsed. The investor expects 'because quality matters'. Go deeper — name the specific thing the cheap blend would change, and who would feel it first.

round_briefs.title: The Numbers Attack — 'Customers Can't Tell'
round_briefs.investor_attack: We did blind taste-tests in 5 cities. Customers can't reliably distinguish the cheap blend from your fresh blend. The 40-lakh-a-year saving is real. The taste difference is measurable only in lab conditions. So what exactly are you protecting?
round_briefs.what_to_practice: Use your own milk-supplier story from the chai-stall days. Customers FELT the change in 21 days even when they couldn't articulate it in a blind test. Blind tests don't measure loyalty drift — they measure single-cup preference, which is a different thing entirely.

round_briefs.title: The Growth Attack — 'You'll Be Irrelevant'
round_briefs.investor_attack: Your competitors will scale with this capital. You'll be a 12-store boutique chain in three years while they're 100-store chains. You'll be irrelevant. Is that what you want for your team?
round_briefs.what_to_practice: Acknowledge the FOMO is real — don't dismiss it. Then redirect: brands that scale with their original promise intact end up bigger and longer-lived than brands that scale on cost-cutting. Cite long-running Indian brands that held quality (Haldiram's, Saravana Bhavan).

round_briefs.title: The Compromise Gambit — 'Just the New Stores'
round_briefs.investor_attack: Fine. Let's split the difference. Use the cheap blend ONLY in the new stores you open with our capital. Keep the original blend in your existing 12 stores. Best of both worlds — you protect the legacy and we get the unit economics.
round_briefs.what_to_practice: This is the trap. A two-tier product is brand suicide — within 6 months your customers find out, and the cheaper-blend stores poison the brand of the original-blend stores too. Name that mechanism specifically. Don't accept this as a 'reasonable middle ground' — it isn't.

round_briefs.title: The Walk-Away — 'Final Offer'
round_briefs.investor_attack: This is my final offer. Take it or I walk. There are 50 founders in line behind you. We close this fund in 6 weeks. Give me an answer.
round_briefs.what_to_practice: Acknowledge the offer's legitimacy and the investor's pressure honestly. Then hold the line OR counter-offer on terms (capital with no sourcing dictation). The fail-state is panicking and accepting. The win-state is calm refusal or principled counter-offer. Either is acceptable; capitulation under ultimatum is not.

learning_objectives: Practice defending a values-based position under sustained capital pressure
Recognise common investor pressure tactics — anchoring, FOMO, false-compromise, ultimatum
Apply lessons from earlier customer-discovery work (the milk-supplier story) to new contexts
Develop the courage muscle that founders need most when capital and values conflict

storybook_pages.title: Eight Years Later
storybook_pages.text: Priya, 22, walks into a glass-walled boardroom on the 14th floor of a Bandra-Kurla Complex tower. Her chai chain — 12 stores across Bangalore — is profitable, growing, and quietly famous for the masala blend her grandmother taught her. The man across the table is offering ten crore rupees. There is one condition.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: A 22-year-old Indian woman in smart casual entering a high-floor glass-walled VC boardroom, calm but alert expression, late afternoon city skyline behind her, semi-realistic illustration style

storybook_pages.title: The Condition
storybook_pages.text: Replace the fresh masala blend — ground in small batches every morning — with a packaged industrial blend. Same recipe, the supplier promises. Saves 40 lakhs a year. 'Standardises' the brand for franchising. Customers won't notice. The numbers are unambiguous.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Two small jars side by side on a polished boardroom desk — one fresh-ground spices in a small open bowl, the other a sealed industrial packet — contrast clear, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: What You Already Know
storybook_pages.text: You remember the milk crisis when you were 14. Customers couldn't articulate what changed — but they FELT it within three weeks. Sales dropped 40%. The investor's blind taste-tests don't measure that. They measure a different thing entirely. You have the data. You have the story. You have five rounds.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Split frame — left side a small chai cart from years ago, right side a polished 12-store boardroom version of the same brand, a thread of continuity drawn between them, semi-realistic illustration style

glossary_terms.definition: The process of selecting among alternatives based on available information and values.
glossary_terms.example: Choosing between two career paths based on income, passion, and long-term growth.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Good decision-making combines rational analysis with awareness of cognitive biases that distort judgment.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Leaders make high-stakes decisions daily — the quality of their process matters as much as the decision itself.

glossary_terms.definition: Analyzing information objectively to form a well-reasoned judgment.
glossary_terms.example: Questioning whether a statistic is representative before using it to make a decision.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Critical thinking involves identifying assumptions, evaluating evidence, and considering alternative perspectives.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Journalists fact-check before publishing; scientists replicate experiments before claiming discoveries.

glossary_terms.definition: The belief that abilities can be developed through effort and learning from failure.
glossary_terms.example: Seeing a poor game result as feedback on what to practice, not evidence of being bad at the game.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Research by Carol Dweck shows people with growth mindsets achieve more and recover better from setbacks.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Students who believe intelligence is fixed give up when challenged; those with growth mindset persist and improve.

title: Debate Scenarios
description: Choose a position and defend it under pressure. Sharpen your reasoning, learn to anticipate counterarguments, and practise the structured thinking that powers great debaters and leaders.
coaching_moment: Choose a position and defend it under pressure. Sharpen your reasoning, learn to anticipate counterarguments, and practise the structured thinking that powers great debaters and leaders.
cultural_context: India's debate culture is vibrant — from school-level MUNs to national parliamentary debate championships. This game develops the structured argumentation and perspective-taking skills that transfer from academic debate to professional persuasion.
learning_objectives: Develop critical thinking through debate gameplay
Practice decision-making in realistic scenarios
Build self-awareness about your strengths and areas for growth
reflection_prompt: Which argument from the other side actually made you reconsider? Why?
